lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Owned the claims backlog report and the weekly numbers the claims managers used.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Improved reporting efficiency by 90% by moving the monthly revenue report to scheduled SQL queries.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.
- Wrote data-quality checks on the 40 most-used tables, catching 15 broken loads before they reached a dashboard.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Reported the national conversion rate as the simple average of 14 regional conversion rates, without weighting by regional traffic.
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Compared the forecast with the operator's rebalancing schedule: empty-station hours fell from 310 to 205 a week in a replay of last summer.
- Published the notebooks and a short write-up, which the city's open-data team linked from its bike-share page.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Built a retention dashboard for about 2.4 million shoppers that raised repeat purchases by nearly a quarter.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: The résumé includes date of birth and nationality.
items.because: These details do not help a reader assess analyst work and are normally left off a résumé.

items.says: Experience is not ordered newest-first.
items.because: Pinecrest appears before the later Brightcart role, so readers must skip the older job to find the most recent analyst work.

items.says: Education appears before the analyst work that makes the stronger introduction.
Paid employment ends in June 2025, and the ongoing independent project does not account for a subsequent role.
“Owned” states responsibility without showing the reporting or analysis performed.
“The weekly numbers” neither names the figures nor says what managers used them to do.
The call-center analysis does not identify the analysis behind the staffing recommendation.
The call-center result is stronger than the bullet currently placed first.
“My findings” introduces a first-person pronoun into the bullet.
“By half” does not reveal how many query errors the SQL guide eliminated.
items.because: Without comparable before-and-after counts, a reader cannot gauge the result’s weight.

items.says: Unrelated duties separate the fraud-flag automation from its 10-hour monthly saving.
items.because: The intervening list makes it unclear which activity produced the saving and makes the automation result harder to spot.

items.says: The automation claim does not say what part of the fraud-flag extract process it replaced.
“Reporting efficiency” does not identify what improved by 90%.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the figure describes preparation time, manual steps or another measure.

items.says: “By 90% by moving” repeats the same connector.
Left-joining orders to customers and counting null customer names does not find customers with no orders.
items.because: Starting from orders excludes customers who have never ordered, and a null name could mean an unmatched order or a missing name.

items.says: “Data-quality checks” does not show what the checks tested.
Presenting the customer review does not show what analysis produced its recommendations.
items.because: A reader sees the presentation and funding outcome but not the analytical contribution.

items.says: The funded recommendations are not identified.
The presentation comes before the funding result, delaying the strongest part of the line.
The simple average of regional conversion rates is not generally the national conversion rate.
items.because: An equal average gives low-traffic and high-traffic regions the same weight, whereas the national rate divides total conversions by total traffic.

items.says: The strongest Brightcart result is not the entry’s opening bullet.
items.because: The retention work combines a defined audience, a marketing use and a before-and-after result.

items.says: The dashboard bullet does not explain how it identified lapsed buyers.
items.because: The rule behind the audience is missing, so the analysis is hard to distinguish from routine dashboard assembly.

items.says: The rise in 90-day repeat purchase comes too late in the bullet.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the measurable result after the dashboard and its use are described.

items.says: “12% mean absolute error” incorrectly expresses mean absolute error as a percentage.
items.because: Mean absolute error for hourly trip counts is measured in trips; a percentage requires a separately defined percentage-error or normalized metric.

items.says: The bike-share demand bullet does not name the forecasting approach.
The forecast accuracy has no baseline for comparison.
The replay bullet does not identify the forecast-guided rebalancing change tested.
items.because: Without that step between forecasting and the reduction in empty-station hours, a reader cannot tell what decision the analysis contributed.

items.says: “310 to 205 a week” makes the weekly unit easy to miss.
“So the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut” leaves the actor unclear and states the result conversationally.
Matching repeat visitors does not, by itself, produce a count of unique households.
items.because: A household can include multiple visitors, so counting households requires a way to group visitors by household.

items.says: “Matched repeat visitors” does not identify the matching rule.
“Its first count of unique households” does not provide the count.
The shopper dashboard and repeat-purchase claim duplicates the retail retention result and does not fit the pantry project.
items.because: Attributing what appears to be the same retail-scale result to two entries undermines confidence in both and leaves its connection to pantry records unclear.
